Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:67: And in the Zohar (Parashat Mishpatim 122a), in these words: we have learned, Israel is called "holy," and because they are holy, it is forbidden for people to call their fellow by a disgraceful name, or to give a nickname to their fellow, and his punishment is great, all the more so with other, worse words. Rabbi Yosei said, whoever calls his fellow by a name he does not have, and thereby shames him, is caught by [being accused of] what he himself does not have — for Rabbi Chiya said in the name of Rabbi Chizkiah, whoever calls his fellow "wicked," they bring him down to Gehinnom and bring down his descendants — except for the insolent ones of the Torah [i.e., known transgressors], where the Torah permits a person to call them wicked — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:68: Now, having discussed the divisions of evil speech according to what is found in the books, we must explain the punishment of one who accepts evil speech. In tractate Pesachim (118a) it says: Rav Sheshet said in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, whoever tells evil speech, whoever accepts evil speech, and whoever testifies falsely against his fellow deserves to be thrown to the dogs, as it is said, "you shall cast it to the dogs" (Exodus 22:30), and adjacent to it, "you shall not accept a false report" (Exodus 23:1) — so far his words. And in the Mechilta they say, "keep far from a false matter" (Exodus 23:7) — this is a warning to those who accept evil speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:69: Further, they say in Pesachim (87b): why did Jeroboam merit to be counted among the kings of Israel and Judah? Because he did not accept evil speech, and so on — see there. We also find that David's accepting evil speech from Ziba against Mephibosheth caused the kingdom of the house of David to be divided, as we learn in tractate Shabbat (56b): they say, of blessed memory: Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, at the time David said to Mephibosheth, "you and Ziba shall divide the field" (II Samuel 19:30), a heavenly voice went out and said, "Rehoboam and Jeroboam shall divide the kingdom." If, in a case where the matters were clearly discernible, he still came to believe the matter, and such a great breach resulted from the cause of accepting evil speech, all the more so must a person distance himself and stop up his ears from hearing the evil speech told every day about innocent people.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:70: Whoever accepts evil speech and shows in his soul that he agrees with the teller and believes the words in front of people is as though he had told it himself, for he assists the evil and causes disgrace to his fellow — for when the informer sees the listener's face grow angry, he stops his words, but if he sees that the listener will accept it, he will not hold back his lies. Therefore we were warned, "you shall not accept a false report" — that we should not believe in our hearts the report of evil speech, so as to hold in our minds that those words are true, to demean the one about whom they were said, God forbid.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:71: In Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Zuta, ch. 7), they say, of blessed memory: they said of Jeroboam son of Joash that he was accustomed to honoring prophets, and what the Holy One, blessed be He, did not hand over through the hand of Joshua son of Nun or through the hand of David king of Israel, He handed over through his hand, as it is said, "he restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Chamath to the sea of the Aravah" (II Kings 14:25). Similarly you say, "for the Lord saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter, and there was none shut up, nor any left, nor any helper for Israel; and the Lord did not say that He would blot out the name of Israel" (II Kings 14:26-27) — and what was Jeroboam's merit in this matter? Was Jeroboam not an idol worshiper? Rather, it was because he did not accept evil speech regarding the prophet Amos, as it is said, "then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos has conspired against you... thus Amos says, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land" (Amos 7:10-11) — he immediately rebuked him and threw him out in a reprimand, saying, "God forbid, that righteous man did not prophesy this prophecy, and if he did prophesy, it was not of his own mind but from Heaven." At that hour the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "A generation of idol worshipers, the head of the generation an idol worshiper, yet he did not accept evil speech — the land which I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your seed I will give it,' I will give into his hand," and he restored the border of Israel — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:72: Further, among the things that blemish the covenant of the tongue, related to the matter of evil speech, is that one must be careful not to curse one's fellow using the Name — even without mentioning the Lord, but merely in a foreign tongue, it is forbidden and transgresses a negative commandment, and even to utter a curse from one's mouth unintentionally is not fitting, for "a covenant has been made with the lips" (Mo'ed Katan 18a); and many have been punished for this, as it is said in the Gemara several times (ibid.), "it is like an inadvertent error that goes forth from before a ruler."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:73: It says in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach 175a), regarding the death of Rachel, that our father Jacob, peace be upon him, caused her death by cursing unintentionally, in these words: Rabbi Yosei said, it is written, "an undeserved curse shall not come (lo tavo)" (Proverbs 26:2), but they established it as "lo" spelled with a Vav [meaning "shall come to him"] — and if it is the curse of a righteous person, even if he did not intend it, once it leaves his mouth, that evil inclination takes it and accuses through it at a time of danger. Jacob said, "with whomever you find your gods, he shall not live" (Genesis 31:32) — and even though he did not know [that Rachel had them], that evil accuser found among people always took that word up. Therefore we have learned, a person should never open his mouth to Satan, because he takes that word and accuses through it above and below — all the more so a word of a sage or a word of a righteous person — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:74: Likewise they say, of blessed memory, in tractate Makkot (11a): Rabbi Abahu said, the curse of a sage comes to pass even if there is no reason for it — from where do we learn this? From Eli, who said to Samuel (I Samuel 3:17), "so may God do to you and more also, if you hide anything from me" — and although it is written, "and Samuel told him all the things and did not hide them from him," it is [nevertheless] written, "and his sons did not walk in his ways" (I Samuel 8:3). And they bring another proof there, which we shall not quote so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:75: Likewise of this category is that one should not curse one who does not hear it, as the Targum explains regarding "you shall not curse a deaf person" (Leviticus 19:14) — "you shall not curse one who does not hear it." And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim 85a): come and see, whoever curses his fellow while he is in front of him and shames him, it is as though he shed his blood, and this has already been established. But this verse [refers to] one whose fellow is not with him, and he curses him with that word — and there is not a single word that goes forth from a person's mouth that has no voice, and that voice ascends above, and how many accusers join together with that voice, until it ascends and arouses the place of the great abyss, as they have established, and how many are aroused against that person! Woe to whoever utters an evil word from his mouth, and this has already been established — so far his words. And the pious author writes in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of the Love of God, ch. 6) how much common people are disgraced by uttering curses and blasphemies from their mouths.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:76: Further, one must be careful not to curse oneself in anger, for in the fourth chamber of the chambers of the kelipot there are powers called "cursers of the day," and they take that curse a person cursed himself with and fulfill it, God forbid (Parashat Pekudei 266a). This is one of the three that cause harm to themselves, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit 14b, and likewise 8b) — that David, because he said, "the man who has done this deserves to die" (II Samuel 12:5), was seized upon by Duma, and had the Holy One, blessed be He, not helped him, he would have fallen into Duma's hand, as King David, peace be upon him, said, "unless the Lord had been my help, my soul had almost dwelt in silence (duma)" (Psalms 94:17).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:77: Concerning something similar they said, of blessed memory, that a person should never open his mouth to Satan, as we learn in the chapter Mi SheMeto (Berachot 19a), in these words: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, and so it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosei, a person should never open his mouth to Satan. Rav Yosef said, what is the verse? As it is said, "we were almost as Sodom" (Isaiah 1:9) — what did the prophet answer him? "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom" (Isaiah 1:10). And it further says there, above this, that for this reason the mourner should not say, in justifying the divine judgment (tzidduk hadin), "Master of the universe, I have sinned greatly before You, and You have not exacted from me one part in a thousand." Likewise it is fitting that one not curse his wife, for the male is half a body, and both together are one complete person — and if he curses her, he is found cursing himself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:78: It seems to me that the warning for all these aspects comes from the verse, "and make no mention of the name of other gods" (Exodus 23:13) — for all the blemishes of the tongue are from the side of the outsider, which is "other gods." And so King David, peace be upon him, said, "guard your tongue from evil (ra)" — the intent being that all the matters that have a grip toward "evil," which is Samael, [should be guarded against]. And when he guards his tongue, he will merit life and good, as it says, "Who is the man who desires life, who loves days..." (Psalms 34:13).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:79: And with this, this chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:1: Now, having discussed, in the preceding chapters, the matter of the four classes who do not receive the presence of the Shechinah, it remains for us to explain, in this chapter, the matter of vows and oaths that depend on speech, and likewise all the other things that blemish speech.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:2: Regarding the matter of oaths, Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, writes in the book Menorat HaMa'or (ch. 1, letter 38), in these words: those who swear by the Name, blessed be He, mean to say that just as He, blessed be He, is true, so their words are true, whether past or future; and one who swears falsely is like one who denies the truth of the Name. And if a person swears by the head of a king of flesh and blood and does not fulfill his word, he deserves death, because he demeans the king's honor — and if this is fitting to be done to one who swears by a king of flesh and blood, who came from a putrid drop and is destined to die, all the more so must a person guard his mouth and tongue so as not to stumble into causing his flesh to sin by swearing falsely by the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who is living and enduring forever. We already know what happened to the children of Israel because they swore publicly regarding the matter of the concubine in Gibeah, and likewise the famine the Name brought upon the land because of Saul and his household, who transgressed the oath of the princes that they swore to the Gibeonites (Bamidbar Rabbah 5:3). And we see that no explicit punishment is written among the warnings in the Ten Commandments except for idolatry and "you shall not bear [the Name in vain]," and yet people are so accustomed to this matter that some transgress it a hundred times a day with no benefit gained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:3: Because people are not well versed in the severity of the oath and its great weight, they come to blind their own eyes and swear falsely; therefore our Rabbis instituted that the court, in every era, should make known to the one taking an oath the severity of the oath and its law, in a language he understands, in order to open his ear, so that perhaps he will fear and withdraw from the oath — as we learn in tractate Shevuot (38b): our Rabbis taught, the oath of judges is likewise said in its own language; they say to him, know that the whole world trembled when the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "you shall not bear the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Exodus 20:7), and for all the transgressions in the Torah, retribution is exacted from him [alone], but here from him and from his family, as it is said, "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" (Ecclesiastes 5:5), and "your flesh" refers only to your relative, as it is said, "and do not hide yourself from your own flesh" (Isaiah 58:7). And for all the transgressions in the Torah, retribution is exacted from him [alone], but here from him and from the whole world, as it is said, "swearing, and lying..." (Hosea 4:2), and it is written, "therefore the land mourns" (Hosea 4:3). And for all the transgressions in the Torah, if he has merit, they suspend [punishment] for two or three generations, but here retribution is exacted from him immediately, as it is said, "I will send it forth, says the Lord, and it shall enter into the house of the thief" (Zechariah 5:4) — "I will send it forth" immediately, "and it shall enter into the house of the thief" — this refers to one who steals his fellow's mind, having no money owed to him and yet demanding it and making him swear; "and into the house of him who swears falsely by My name" is according to its plain meaning; "and it shall remain in the midst of his house, and shall consume it with its timber and its stones" — this teaches that there are things that fire and water do not consume, but a false oath consumes them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:4: Further, we find that the sin of a false oath is equated with the desecration of the Name, as it is said (Avot 5:9), "wild beasts come into the world because of false oaths and because of the desecration of the Name." Further, we learn in the Sifrei, on "and you shall not swear by My name falsely" (Leviticus 19:12): why is this stated? Since it says, "you shall not bear the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Exodus 20:7), one might think this obligation applies only regarding the unique Name [YHVH] alone — from where do we include all the other appellations? The verse teaches, "by My name" — any name that is Mine. "And you shall profane the name" — this teaches that a false oath is a desecration of the Lord. We learn in the Midrash Tanchuma: whoever betrays [trust regarding] oaths denies the Holy One, blessed be He, and has no forgiveness forever, as it is said, "for [the Lord] will not hold him guiltless" (Exodus 20:7) — so far his words. I have abridged his words to what is needed for our purpose, so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:5: Further, we learn in Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Matot), in these words: "if a man vows a vow to the Lord" (Numbers 30:3) — this is what is written, "and you shall swear, As the Lord lives, in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness" (Jeremiah 4:2). The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: do not think it is permitted for you to swear by My Name — even in truth you are not permitted to swear by My Name unless all these qualities are in you: "you shall fear the Lord your God" (Deuteronomy 10:20) — that you be like those who were called "God-fearing": Abraham, Job, and Joseph. Abraham, as it is written, "for now I know that you fear God" (Genesis 22:12); Job, as it is written, "a plain and upright man, who feared God" (Job 1:1); Joseph, as it is written, "I fear God" (Genesis 42:18) — this is "you shall fear the Lord your God." "And Him shall you serve" — if you dedicate yourself to Torah and occupation with the commandments and have no other occupation, therefore it says, "and Him shall you serve." "And to Him shall you cleave" — but can a person cleave to the Shechinah? Is it not already said, "for the Lord your God is a consuming fire" (Deuteronomy 4:24)? Rather, [it means] to teach you: whoever marries his daughter to a Torah scholar who reads and studies, and does business for him, and benefits him from his possessions, is the one of whom it is said, "and to Him shall you cleave." If you have all these qualities, you are permitted to swear; if not, you are not permitted to swear. There is a story of King Yannai, who had two thousand towns, all of which were destroyed because of true oaths! How so? A person would say to his fellow, by oath, "I will go and eat such-and-such in such-and-such a place, and drink such-and-such in such-and-such a place," and they would go and fulfill their oaths, and [in doing so, wasting resources,] they were destroyed. And if one who swears truly [suffers this], all the more so one who swears falsely! — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:6: On the verse "lo tissa" ("you shall not bear") (Exodus 20:7), they explain in the Mechilta, in these words: why is "lo tissa" stated? Since it says, "and you shall not swear by My name falsely" (Leviticus 19:12), I would know only that one should not swear [falsely] — from where do we learn that one should not accept upon himself to swear [an oath at all, casually]? The verse teaches, "you shall not bear the name of the Lord your God" — before you accept upon yourself to swear, I am, as it were, your God [in an ordinary relationship]; once you accept upon yourself to swear, I am, as it were, your judge — as it is said, "for the Lord will not hold guiltless him who bears His name in vain." It is impossible to say "He will not hold guiltless," since it is already said, "and He clears (venakeh) [the guilty]" (Exodus 34:7), and it is impossible to say "He clears," since it is already said, "He will not hold guiltless"; say from this point on: He clears those who repent, but does not clear those who do not repent — so far their words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:7: According to the plain sense, "lo tissa" means that a person should not habitually "bear" (carry, mention) the Name of Heaven in his mouth in vain, in the manner of "nor will I take up (esa) their names upon my lips" (Psalms 16:4) — and so Ramban, peace be upon him, explains.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:8: And in the Tikkunim (118a), regarding the severity of the sin of oaths, they say, in these words: but others, from whose mouths go forth the "breaths" of an oath, concerning them it is said, "for she has cast down many wounded" (Proverbs 7:26), and these are called "wounded" (chalalim), for they desecrate (mechalelim) the Name of the Lord and utter "breaths" from their mouths. And likewise those whose speech is falsehood, and swearing falsely, and mentioning His Name in vain and falsely — with that Name that they utter in vain and falsehood, they build structures that are nullified from the world — this is what is written, "in vain I have struck your children" (Jeremiah 2:30). Woe to those people who utter from their mouths words and oaths of falsehood — it would be better for them not to have come into the world! All the colleagues rose and said, "May the Merciful One save us! May the Merciful One save us!" — so far their words. Also in the Zohar (Parashat Yitro 87b, 91b), in explaining this verse, they elaborate at length on the severity of the sin, but we shall not quote it, so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:9: In the book Ta'amei HaMitzvot by the sage Rabbi Yitzchak ben Farchia, peace be upon him, he explains the severity of the oath in the commandment "lo tissa," in these words: "you shall not bear the name of the Lord your God in vain" — for whoever swears falsely cuts off and separates the groom from the bride — this being "lo tissa" ("you shall not bear/lift"), that you not lift YHVH away from your God [Elohim, the Shechinah]. Because one who swears falsely blemishes this seventh attribute, his punishment is so severe — "and shall consume it with its timber and its stones" — and therefore adjacent to it comes "Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" (Exodus 20:8), for the Sabbath is the male [aspect], and one must sanctify it and not separate it, God forbid. Further he writes that one who swears is as though he takes hold of the precious object of the supernal Covenant in his hand — the proof being "put now your hand under my thigh" (Genesis 24:2) — and if, God forbid, he swears in vain and falsely, he cuts off and separates.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:10: Further, I have heard in the name of the Kabbalists that the verse "lo tissa" has seventeen words, equal in number to "tov" (good), and to YHVH by the small reckoning, and to "Torah," and to "seven" — to hint that one who swears falsely is uprooted from the good of the World to Come and from the other things mentioned, and from the sevenths alluded to in the oath (shevu'ah, sharing the root of "seven") — for "shevuah" written defectively [without a Vav] and vocalized equals sixty-six, equal to Adonai plus the sum of its letters.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:11: Also included in the matter of the oath, one must be careful about mentioning the Name of Heaven in vain, for whoever mentions it in vain is liable to excommunication (Nedarim 7b), and this is included in "lo tissa" as explained. Whoever is careful of this has a great reward in the World to Come, as it is written, "but unto you who fear My name shall the sun of righteousness arise" (Malachi 3:20), and they explain in Nedarim (8b), "these are people who fear to utter the Name of Heaven in vain" — so far their words. The explanation of "sun of righteousness" is explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 13.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:12: Also included in [prohibitions regarding] an oath is that one should not extend his hand to his beard and swear, for this is [equivalent to] an oath, as explained in the Idra Naso (end of 131a), in these words: whoever extends his hand to his beard to swear is like one who swears by the thirteen rectifications of the Beard — so far his words. Also one should be careful not to swear "by truth," for YHVH is called truth, as it is said, "but the Lord God is truth" (Jeremiah 10:10). And likewise one should be careful not to swear "by my soul's life," for the soul is a part of God above, and thus it is found equivalent to swearing by the Name.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:13: Further, it is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 416, and siman 891) that one should not say, "So may I merit the life of the World to Come, if this is not so." It is further written there (siman 420) that in this era one should not swear to fulfill commandments, for Satan will accuse him and he will not fulfill his oath; and there is support for this from the passage of Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Matot) that we quoted above, which said, "you shall fear the Lord your God, Him shall you serve..." — if you have all these qualities, you may swear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:14: Regarding the sin of vows, they say in tractate Nedarim (20a): it was taught, a person should never be accustomed to making vows, for you will eventually betray oaths [through carelessness bred by habit]. Further, we learn there (22a): the son of Rabbi Yannai the Elder's daughter came before Rabbi Yannai the Great; he said to him, "If you had known that your ledger is opened and your deeds examined, would you have made a vow?" And it further says there: what did Rabban Gamliel open with to that elder? "There is one who speaks rashly, like the piercings of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is health" (Proverbs 12:18). Further there: whoever speaks rashly deserves to be pierced with a sword, but the tongue of the wise is health. Further there, it was taught, Rabbi Natan says, whoever makes a vow is as though he built a high place [an illegitimate altar], and whoever fulfills it is as though he offered a sacrifice [upon it], and so on; and one who fulfills it without inquiring about his vow [with a sage] is as though he offered upon that high place, liable for [the sin of] sacrificing outside [the Temple].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:15: Further there, Shmuel said, whoever makes a vow, even though he fulfills it, is called wicked. Rabbi Abahu said, what is the verse? "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall be no sin in you" (Deuteronomy 23:23), and he derives "refrain" from "refrain" [elsewhere]: it is written here, "but if you refrain from vowing," and it is written there, "there the wicked cease (chadelu) from troubling" (Job 3:17) — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:16: In chapter 10 (Nedarim 77b) we learn: Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, taught, whoever makes a vow, even though he fulfills it, is called a sinner. Rav Zevid said, what is the verse? "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall be no sin in you" — implying that if you do not refrain, there is a sin — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:17: Further there, they say in tractate Shabbat (32b): it was taught, Rabbi Natan says, because of the sin of vows, a person's wife dies, as it is said, "if you have nothing to pay, why should he take away your bed from under you?" (Proverbs 22:27). Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] says, because of the sin of vows, children die while young, as it is said, "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error; why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands?" (Ecclesiastes 5:5) — and these are the work of a person's hands: his sons and daughters — so far his words, as pertains to us. The reason for this is that vows are in the supernal Imma, as explained in Ra'aya Meheimna, and one must fulfill his vow and bring it to the place of action, which is the Shechinah; and if, God forbid, he does not fulfill it, the sin is in the children and in the lower Imma [the Shechinah], and therefore his wife dies.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:18: In the Midrash Kohelet (Rabbah 5:3), they explain this verse regarding those who pledge charity publicly and do not give. Incidentally we shall quote the severity of the sin of vows, explained above (Kohelet Rabbah 5:2), on the verse "it is better that you should not vow": Rav Huna said, there was a story of a man who made a vow and did not fulfill it, and set sail on the great sea, and his ship sank at sea and he died. Rabbi Shmuel said, whoever makes a vow and does not fulfill it causes his own wife to die, as it is written, "and as for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died with (upon) me" (Genesis 48:7). And so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach 175a): Jacob was punished for a vow he did not fulfill, and this was harder for Jacob than all the troubles that came upon him. And how do we know it was because of Jacob? Because it is written, "Rachel died upon me" — "upon me," certainly, because I delayed my vow — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:19: Further there, in the Midrash, Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, whoever makes a vow and does not fulfill it causes himself to come to transgression — idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed — and all learn this from Jacob: idolatry, as it is written, "remove the foreign gods that are among you" (Genesis 35:2); forbidden relations, as it is written, "for he had defiled Dinah their sister" (Genesis 34:27); bloodshed, as it is written, "and the two sons of Jacob took..." (Genesis 34:25); and evil speech, as it is written, "and he heard the words of Laban's sons" (Genesis 31:1). Rabbi Muna said, whoever makes a vow and does not fulfill it causes death for himself, as it is said, "for the Lord your God will surely require it of you" (Deuteronomy 23:22). And Rabbi Ami said, there is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity — no death without sin, as it is said, "the soul that sins, it shall die" (Ezekiel 18:20); and no suffering without iniquity, as it is said, "then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes" (Psalms 89:33).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:20: "Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" — Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets this verse regarding those who pledge charity publicly and do not give. "And do not say before the angel" — this is the cantor — "that it was an error" — "let it be my [carelessness]." "Why should God be angry at your voice" — at that voice you spoke; "and destroy the work of your hands" — the few commandments that are in that man's hand, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings a curse into them and destroys them from him — so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:21: In the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Arachin) this passage of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani is brought, who said that whoever makes a vow and delays fulfilling it eventually comes to idolatry, forbidden relations, bloodshed, and evil speech, and he proves all this from Jacob as stated in the passage. It further says there: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, whoever makes a vow and pays it has a reward for the vowing and for the payment, as it is said, "vow and pay unto the Lord your God" (Psalms 76:12); and whoever makes a vow and delays it causes his own death, as it is written, "for the Lord your God will surely require it of you" — from you [himself] it is exacted, not from your money [alone]. Rabbi Ami said, there is no death without sin — so far his words, as pertains to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:22: It seems to me that the end of the verse, "and it shall be a sin in you," can be understood in the manner explained in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot 75b), "that He see no ervat davar in you" (Deuteronomy 23:15), explained above (ch. 11) to mean that that very sin becomes literally portrayed in his body — in this same manner, "He will surely require it," which they explain, of blessed memory, [to mean] death, because speech creates an actual reality within his body, in which the sin is marked; this is [the meaning of] "and it shall be in you" — the sin itself shall be in you — and therefore retribution is exacted from you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:23: There is no doubt that what is said, that whoever makes a vow and pays it has a reward for the vow and the payment, refers to vows of commandments, consecrated items, or Torah — and the verse is precise in saying "unto the Lord your God," and further the verse says "all around Him" [homiletically applied] — for a vow or oath is given only to one who fears Heaven, who is "around" the Holy One, blessed be He, in the manner of "it shall be very tempestuous round about Him" (Psalms 50:3), which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain (Yevamot 121b) to teach that the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with the righteous to a hair's breadth — and this is also proven from the passage we quoted above from Midrash Rabbah (Parashat Matot).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:24: Further, we learn in Midrash Eichah (Rabbati 2:14), on the verse "they sit upon the ground" (Lamentations 2:10): Rabbi Elazar said, do not take the passage of vows lightly in your eyes, for through the passage of vows the Great Sanhedrin of Zedekiah were killed, and so on — and the rest of the story, see there, so as not to be lengthy; and this story is also brought in Nedarim (65a), with a slight variation between them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:25: Rabbeinu Yaakov writes (Yoreh De'ah, siman 203) that if people are pledging charity publicly and one must pledge with them, he should say "without a vow"; however, if it is a commandment incumbent on him personally and obligatory, such as one who says "I will study this chapter" or "I will study this tractate," and he fears that he might become lax in the matter, though it is within his power to fulfill it, it is permitted for the one making the vow, to spur himself on. For Rav Gidal said, from where do we learn that one may swear to fulfill a commandment? As it is said, "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to keep Your righteous judgments" (Psalms 119:106). All the more so where he is habitually forgetful and transgresses one of the negative commandments, or is lax in fulfilling a positive commandment — it is permitted for him to vow and swear to be strict with himself to keep and fulfill the commandments; and concerning this our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 3:13), "vows are a fence for separation." But from all other vows a person must distance himself greatly — so far his words. We have already written above that it is not fitting to swear or vow even to fulfill a commandment, unless the person is one who fears Heaven and will fulfill his vow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:26: In the Midrash Bereshit Rabbah, on the verse "and Jacob vowed a vow, saying" (Genesis 28:20), they explain that it is permitted and good for one to vow at a time of distress, to perform a commandment and the like, in these words: "and Jacob vowed a vow, saying" — it is written, "which my lips uttered and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress" (Psalms 66:14). Rabbi Yitzchak the Babylonian said, "and my mouth spoke when I was in distress" — that he vowed a commandment at the time of his distress. What is "saying"? For generations, so that they [his descendants] would vow at their time of distress. Jacob opened with a vow first, therefore whoever makes a vow should hang the vow only on him. Rabbi Abahu said, it is written, "who swore to the Lord, vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob" (Psalms 132:2) — "to the Mighty One of Abraham," "to the Mighty One of Isaac" is not written here, but "to the Mighty One of Jacob" — he hung the vow on the one who opened with it first — so far his words. Nevertheless, it is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 403) that whoever is in distress should not make a vow, but should think it over and take counsel before doing so, so that the matter be one he can fulfill.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:27: Know that whoever vows to fulfill a commandment or to occupy himself with Torah for so many hours a day and the like, it is not fitting to have his vow annulled unless he shows the court that he is under great duress; and if they annul it for him without there being a great duress, from Heaven they do not annul it for him — this is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, were precise about in saying (Nedarim 8a), "a great vow he has vowed to the God of Israel," that the Holy One, blessed be He, might say, "What wrong have you found in Me, that you have distanced yourself from Me?" It is like the parable of a person who says to a king of flesh and blood, "By your head, my lord, on such-and-such a day I will bring you such-and-such a gift" — if he does not bring it, his head becomes forfeit to the king, unless the king knows he was under duress. The matter of occupation with Torah or a commandment is literally a gift to the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and one who is lenient and annuls his vow is lenient with the honor of the King of the universe — unlike annulling one's own vow such as "I will eat" or "I will not eat," where it is a mitzvah to inquire about his vow, since there is no [independent] mitzvah in the matter [of the vow itself].
